events.title: Homeboy Sandman, NAHreally, Loman, & Jesse The Tree
about: Homeboy Sandman, NAHreally, Loman, & Jesse The Tree NYC indie rap legend Homeboy Sandman is joined by NAHreally, Loman, and Jesse The Tree for a night of hip-hop at The Rockwell.

Homeboy Sandman is a Hip-Hop artist from Queens, NY. He is highly revered for his thought-provoking lyrics, impeccable flow, and unmatched authenticity. Over his long-standing career, he has received critical praise from Rolling Stone, Associated Press, Pitchfork, The FADER, XXL Magazine, Complex, NPR, and more. Homeboy Sandman has released albums with notable record labels such as Stones Throw, Rhymesayers, and Mello Music Group, as well as his own imprint Dirty Looks. In addition to his accomplished solo career, Homeboy Sandman is also 1/2 of the legendary Hip-Hop duo Lice alongside Aesop Rock.

NAHreally is a Jersey City-based rapper, beatmaker, and show organizer from Massachusetts. Known for his conversational lyrics and laid back production, he’s steadily built a catalog of 10+ releases since 2016. In that same span, his DIY approach to performing, touring, and putting on shows has made him a fixture in the NYC indie rap scene. His music has been covered by Cabbages, Bandcamp Daily, Hearing Things, Okayplayer, and more. His latest album Extra Cheese is out now on Bandcamp via Three Dollar Pistol.

Jesse The Tree is a rapper and producer from Providence, RI. His clever, layered lyricism and introspective storytelling offer a balance of poetry and relatability rarely found in an MC. Tree has built a name around New England and beyond through a steady stream of independent releases and relentless touring. His solo catalog alongside his work as 1/2 of sleepingdogs with rapper/producer Andrew has turned him into a mainstay in indie rap. His music has been covered by Bandcamp Daily, The Rap Music Plug Podcast, Secret House Against, and more. His latest releases Worm in Heaven (Strange Famous) and Dog Complex (Three Dollar Pistol) offer a glimpse into his versatility and craftsmanship both on the mic and behind the boards.

about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi, Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray, Drums Special Guest, Trumpet Special Guest, Bass Double-click to edit...

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

events.title: The Fringe
about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone, bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood.
Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind.

Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow.

events.title: Bert Seager's Heart of Hearing
about: $15 suggested / $5 with Student ID / 6:30pm start / seated Bert Seager’s Heart of Hearing is a-jazz quartet made up of piano, tenor-saxophone, upright-bass, and drums whose aim is to bring listeners into the heart of improvised jazz. The joyful expression of this musical intimacy, the shimmering transparency of the sound, and the sense that these musicians are as much involved in listening as in playing makes for compelling and memorable performances.

Bert Seager, pianist, composer, recording artist, and educator, has led performances in international jazz festivals in Canada, Peru, Bulgaria, Jordan, Ecuador, Israel, China and Japan. As a composer, he is a three-time recipient of the prestigious MacDowell Colony fellowship, an artists residency program in Peterborough, New Hampshire. He has recorded 18 compact discs which have all been released internationally to critical acclaim. Cadence Magazine says Bert’s music is filled with “effervescent optimism.” And the Boston Globe wrote that his “kind of exuberance makes the jazz world go round.”

Rick DiMuzio, tenor saxophonist, composer, and educator, has performed concerts and clinics throughout the United States, Europe, Central and South America, and Asia. In addition to his performing career, Rick is a full Professor at Berklee College of Music where he teaches ear training, improvisation, saxophone, and ensembles. He earned his doctorate in jazz composition from New England Conservatory, a master’s degree in jazz performance from the Eastman School of Music, and a bachelor’s degree in music education from Indiana University of PA.

Bassist Andrew Schiller, after living in Brooklyn NY, for five years, working as a bandleader and sideman playing jazz and improvised music, came to Boston to earn his doctorate in music from the New England Conservatory in 2020. He is now teaching at Berklee College of Music and Salem State University. Andrew’s debut album, "Tied Together, Not To The Ground," was released in May 2017, and his most recent project is "Sonoran," an 9-part suite for quintet are both on Red Piano Records. These albums feature an adventurous and unique compositional style, blending jazz with contemporary classical, rock, and avant-garde influences.

events.title: Lilypad Jazz Jam
about: $5 - 15 sliding scale admission / 4 - 7pm / all ages We're excited to be welcoming the community into our space to play and listen to music together. The Lilypad Jazz Jam is open to instrumentalists of all levels, we only ask that you come prepared to play at least one or two well known Jazz Standards in the commonly played key. And of course listeners are welcome to come and enjoy the music these spontaneously arranged ensembles will create! Our host will be working with players to make sure everyone gets a chance to get on stage and play something they're comfortable with. We'll have a drum kit, piano, upright bass and guitar/bass amplifiers on the back line. Our stage hosts some of the heaviest players on the planet, come down and catch the vibe!
We have Nic Adams hosting and leading the band to get the night started. Come early, you won't want to miss their performance!

Nic Adams is a multi-instrumentalist, performer, composer, educator, and luthier based in Boston, MA. Specializing in saxophone, drums, guitar, bass, and north Asian folk music, their music pulls from a long list of traditions, from John Coltrane to punk rock and Tuvan throat singing. With this wide array of influences, Nic seeks to create music that synthesizes many different musical points into a cohesive and unique form. Finding common grounds among musical cultures and using them as jumping-off points for new compositions or improvisations is at the core of Nic’s work. Nic is currently pursuing a Master’s at Longy School of Music, gigs in the greater Boston area, and spends their free time building hybrid Tuvan/western traditional instruments.

about: $25 at the door / $20 in advance / $15 students and seniors / 7:30 doors / seated <a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button > Get Tickets Lafayette Gilchrist featuring special guest and Cambridge native, Cecil Brooks of the Sun Ra Arkestra.

Lafayette Gilchrist’s music draws on the span of jazz history from stride to free improvisation, along with inspiration from hip-hop, funk, and Washington D.C.’s unique go-go sound. His work thrives on making surprising connections between styles and influences, boldly veering from piledriver funk to piquant stride, vigorous swing to hip-hop swagger, contemplative abstraction to deep-bottom grooves. Gilchrist is the pianist in the Sun Ra Arkestra, has toured extensively with David Murray, and his compositions have graced the soundtracks of David Simon’s acclaimed series The Wire, The Deuce, and Treme.

Gilchrist has performed with Cassandra Wilson, Macy Gray, Oliver Lake, Andrew Cyrille, Orrin Evans, Paul Dunmall, Hamid Drake, William Parker and many more. Gilchrist’s second solo recording, 2019 “Dark Matter” which muses on the elusive and mysterious matter that ties the universe together, landed on numerous critics best of lists.

Gilchrist returns to The Lilypad, where he played for a standing room only crowd in 2022, for a performance featuring a special guest appearance by Cambridge native and fellow member of the Sun Ra Arkestra, Cecil Brooks on trumpet.

events.title: Jazz Composers Alliance Presents the JCA Orchestra
about: $20 admission / $15 for students and seniors / 1:45 doors / 2pm start New Music for the 21 piece Jazz Orchestra by resident composers David Harris, Darrell Katz, Bob Pilkington and Mimi Rabson.

The Jazz Composers Alliance was founded in 41 years ago to support, develop and promote the art of music composition in the jazz idiom. The JCA Orchestra was founded to realize that goal, and it has been a fixture on Boston’s creative music scene ever since its first performance in December 1985. The JCA Orchestra has released 12 critically acclaimed CDs. Wheelworks was on Downbeat’s Best of 2016 list. The group has performed (and on a few occasions, recorded with) an illustrious group of guest performer/composers, including Sam Rivers, Julius Hemphill, Dave Holland, Maria Schneider, Henry Threadgill, Steve Lacy and Oliver Lake. Drawing on influences that span the history of jazz and the world's musical traditions, the JCA Orchestra has brought together a huge palette of sounds, structures and concepts. This group has premiered well over 125 pieces. Our concepts include extended forms, group improvisation from a variety of approaches, notated and not notated music, and striving to combine composition and improvisation in new ways.

The 21-piece JCA orchestra a string trio, a vocalist, as well as a full-time flute player, and French horn, we’re not a typical big band, We have lasted since 1985, and it’s because we have a like-minded group of people who love making music, who are committed to stretching boundaries, and write and perform with joy and passion. JCA performances have variety, adventure, and a great communal feel.

about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi, Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray, Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest, Trumpet Double-click to edit...

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone, bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood.
Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind.

Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow.

events.detail: with Kenny Werner and John Lockwood
about: $35 admission / 10pm doors / 10:15 music / all ages Peruvian born drummer, percussionist and composer, Jorge Perez-Albela is presenting an unforgettable evening of music improvisation with world class jazz masters, pianist Kenny Werner and bassist John Lockwood.

Kenny has been a world-class pianist and composer for over forty years. His prolific output of compositions, recordings and publications continue to impact audiences around the world. In 1996 he wrote his landmark book, Effortless Mastery, Liberating The Master Musician Within. Werner has since created videos, lectured world-wide and authored many articles on how musicians, artists or even business people can allow their “master creator” within to lift their performance to it’s highest level, showing us how to be spontaneous, fearless, joyful and disciplined in our work and in our life.

Kenny was awarded the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship Award for his seminal work, No Beginning No End. No Beginning No End is a musical journey exploring tragedy and loss, death and transition, and the path from one lifetime to the next. Utilizing over 70 musicians, Kenny’s third album for Half Note Records is an expansive composition featuring Joe Lovano, Judy Silvano, Wind Ensemble, Choir and String Quartet.

Born in Brooklyn, NY on November 19, 1951 and then growing up in Oceanside, Long Island, Kenny began playing and performing at a young age, first recording on television at the age of 11. Although he studied classical piano as a child, he enjoyed playing anything he heard on the radio. In high school and his first years of college he attended the Manhattan School of Music as a classical piano major.

His natural instinct for improvisation led Kenny to the Berklee School of Music in 1970. There he sought tutelage of the renowned piano teacher Madame Chaloff. A Her gracious wisdom and inspiration became a driving force in Kenny’s conception: A music conscious of its spiritual intent and essence.

From Boston, Kenny traveled to Brazil with the saxophonist Victor Assis Brasil. There he met Victor’s twin brother, Brazilian pianist Joao Assis Brasil. He studied with Joao, who provided another piece of the puzzle for Kenny’s conception that would lead to Effortless Mastery, his landmark opus on how to allow the master musician from within to manifest.
John Lockwood was born in Cape Town South Africa.

events.title: SIRINTIP feat. Adam Neely, Matt Wong, Nolan Byrd
about: $14 advance / $18 door / 11pm - 1am / seated & standing <a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button > Buy Tickets Having opened for Wayne Shorter and toured internationally alongside Snarky Puppy and Sungazer, Sirintip comes to Boston for her first headlining performance in the city, celebrating the release of her new EP White Lilies, out October 30. Expect a genre-bending live set spanning cinematic songwriting, vocal effects, improvisation, and high-energy electronic and drum & bass grooves.

FFO: Kimbra, Sungazer, Snarky Puppy, KNOWER, Genevieve Artadi, Hiatus Kaiyote Praised for her depth and dimension, Sirintip creates at the intersection of avant-pop, jazz, and electronic music, combining songwriting and improvisation with electronics, technology, and an ongoing curiosity about the natural world. Her interdisciplinary work expands music beyond the stage through collaborations with scientists, visual artists, and dancers, exploring environmental sustainability and new ways of turning research and data into sound and performance. Her previous albums include Carbon (Ropeadope), named one of DownBeat’s Best Albums of 2022, and Tribus (GroundUP Music), produced by Snarky Puppy’s Michael League and featuring Mark Guiliana. She has toured internationally as a bandleader and alongside Snarky Puppy and Sungazer, with appearances at SFJAZZ, the Nobel Museum, Joe’s Pub, National Sawdust, and Winter Jazzfest.

events.title: Tom Swafford Quartet / John McDonald
about: $15 admission / 3pm doors / 3:30 show / seated / all ages Composer/violinist Tom Swafford presents a set of his solo piano compositions performed by John McDonald. The second set will feature Tom, violin, Brian Price, clarinet and saxophone, Nate McBride, bass, and Curt Newton, drums, performing improvisations based on selected themes and motives from those pieces. The concert will include a set of piano variations on Joann’s Green Satin Dress by Butch Morris, which the improvisors will interpret as well.

Tom played in series of a large ensemble performances led by the esteemed conductor and composer Butch Morris in the fall of 2011. In that series, Morris incorporated his notated works into his practice of Conduction™ (conducted improvisation). This is an inspiration for today’s concert.

John McDonald recently retired after 36 years as composition professor at Tufts University. John was a great inspiration for Tom, who studied with him at Tufts from 1991-1995. In addition to composition instruction, John co-led the NME (New Music Ensemble), which was Tom’s first exposure to free improvisation. Tom has been involved in free improv along with his fully notated composition work since that time.

Prior to Tufts, Tom studied jazz piano and played in his high school jazz ensemble in Seattle. The jazz tradition continues to be an important factor in his compositional approach. Another fun fact is that Tom and Nate McBride played in the band in a Seattle Children’s Theatre production in the late 1980s, when Tom was in 8th grade and Nate was in high school!
Tom is excited to once again collaborate with John, Nate, and this group of excellent Boston area improvisors.

events.title: Allan Chase Quartet ft. Sheryl Bailey
about: $15 admission / 6pm doors / 6:20 start / seated Jazz classics and originals by Chase and Bailey.

Allan Chase is a saxophonist and composer who has performed jazz and improvised music since 1974 with his own groups and as a member of the Lewis Nash-Allan Chase Duo (1979-80), Your Neighborhood Saxophone Quartet (1981-2018), Prima Materia with Rashied Ali (1992-2000), the Steve Lantner Quartet with Joe Morris and Luther Gray, the Bruno Råberg Quartet and Tentet, and the Ayn Inserto Jazz Orchestra. He appears as a soloist on over sixty jazz and improvised music recordings, several rock and classical recordings, and several movie scores.

Chase began teaching at Berklee in 1981 and served as chair of Ear Training there (2008-21). He has also taught at Tufts and NEC, where he served as chair of Jazz Studies, dean of faculty, and chair of Contemporary Improvisation, and continues to teach jazz history courses.

events.title: Joe Hunt Group
about: $15 admission / Start 8:30pm / Doors 8pm / Seated Show Modern jazz played by Boston's best jazz musicians.

Joe Hunt is a jazz drummer, educator, author, and historian. In the early 1960s, Joe Hunt performed and recorded alongside the late NEC Distinguished Artist-in-Residence Emeritus George Russell, with releases on Decca and Riverside. Hunt joined The Stan Getz Quartet in 1964, recording several releases on Verve, then was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1966-1967. The remainder of the 1960s found Hunt performing or recording with several other jazz luminaries including Chet Baker, Eric Dolphy, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Charles Mingus, Bob Brookmeyer, and the late Herb Pomeroy.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Hunt was a member of The National Jazz Ensemble, led jazz groups with John Scofield, Mike Stern, and Santi Debriano, and toured with quartets of Red Rodney and Hal McKusick. The 1990s, and beyond, have included membership in The Smithsonian Jazz Masters Orchestra, with former NEC president Gunther Schuller, performances with Kenny Burrell, Joe Lavano, Joanne Brackeen, and Tal Farlow, as well as recordings with the Bert Seager Quintet, and also, Trio. Hunt is the author of the 1994 book 52nd Street Beat, which is a historical look at jazz drummer greats from 1945 to 1965.

Mark Pinto - alto saxophone, formerly years with the Buddy Rich band John Lockwood – bass, formerly with Joe Henderson, Lee Konitz, current Fringe member Yuka Hamano Hunt – piano, voice, arranger Joe Hunt – drums, formerly with George Russell, Stan Getz, Jim Hall, Dexter Gordon, and Bill Evans We pay tribute to a special composer or performer at most performances. Recent shows have included: Burt Bacharach, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans, and Gigi Gryce. Future shows will include the music of Paul and Carla Bley, and arranger, Johnny Mandel.

events.title: Jesse Gallagher + Steve Fell
about: $10 admission / 7pm / seated show Jesse Gallagher began living above the Lilypad in 2006, just a few blocks from where his grandfather grew up on Inman st. At the time Jesse was in the middle of what would be about a decade of regular touring, performing & recording with his psychedelic rock band Apollo Sunshine. The band was featured in the New York Times, Rolling Stone, Spin & shared the stage with legendary acts Wu-Tang Clan, Toots & The Maytals, The Flaming Lips & Dr. Dog. Jesse has been involved with the Lilypad for 20 years and the full time talent booking agent since 2013.

Breaking Bad used Jesse’s song “We are Born When We Die” (2008) to dramatic effect. “Today is the Day” (2005) was in international Nike commercials while his “Singing to the Earth to Thank Her For You” was used in a large GAP campaign. Gallagher has collaborated, recorded & performed extensively w/ Sam Cohen, Willy Mason, Lilys, Nick Nicely, Doug Tuttle & Edan. Gallagher is a certified Yoga & Meditation teacher and hosts classes at the Lilypad & online. Since 2018, he has released 40 pieces of instrumental music which have been used in millions of YouTube videos ranging from NBC NY to Tesla and most recently a string of viral videos by Emma Chamberlain. Gallagher has a very active YouTube channel, making lots of psychedelic music videos and building a community of mindful listeners.

Steve Fell is a guitarist, composer, and educator whose performing and recording career over the last twenty five years has reached across the boundaries of jazz, experimental, funk, free form improvisation, rock, electronic, reggae/calypso, hip-hop, psych, and many others.
He co-leads the groups Clear Audience, Quantum Banditos, Dome Room, and Astronomico, leads a trio under his own name, and collaborates with numerous bands and artists.

events.title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi, Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray, Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest, Trumpet Double-click to edit...

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone, bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood.
Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind.

Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow.

events.title: Bert Seager's Standard Deviation
about: $15 suggested / $5 with Student ID / 6:30pm start / seated The jazz quintet Standard Deviation, led by pianist and composer Bert Seager, is a tight, two-horn, hard-bop combo that plays his arrangements of jazz standards alongside his own singable originals. The music offers plenty of room for the band to open up and interact. Their special chemistry makes it obvious why sharing jazz in an intimate club like the Lilypad remains such a compelling communal experience.

Bert Seager, pianist, composer, recording artist, and educator, has led performances in international jazz festivals in Canada, Peru, Bulgaria, Jordan, Ecuador, Israel, China and Japan. As a composer, he is a three-time recipient of the prestigious MacDowell Colony fellowship, an artists residency program in Peterborough, New Hampshire. He has recorded 18 compact discs which have all been released internationally to critical acclaim. Cadence Magazine says Bert’s music is filled with “effervescent optimism.” And the Boston Globe wrote that his “kind of exuberance makes the jazz world go round.”

events.title: Eliza Edens & Nora Meier
about: $12 advance / $15 day of show / 9:15 doors / 9:30 music / all ages Brooklyn-based songwriter Eliza Edens celebrates the release of their latest record 'Death Drive.' Local songwriter Nora Meier supports.

<a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button Eliza Edens is a Brooklyn-based songwriter who writes songs that dance inside the white-hot intersection of pleasure and pain. Bold and sincere, their songs are like antique cameo necklaces–snapshots of tenderness, worn close to the heart. A palette of punchy electric guitars and drums, gentle keys, and flourishes of saxophone and electronic percussion accent Edens’ voice as they sing of lovers & lilacs, grief & gratitude, and Freud’s “death drive.” Chameleonic in nature, Edens touches corners of pop, rock, folk, and country–with their voice as the glue that binds each genre foray together into a commanding sound.

Edens came up initially on the DIY songwriter circuit–playing self-booked tours of small clubs and listening rooms on the quiet success of 2020’s Time Away From Time and 2022’s lush acoustic-fingerpicked We’ll Become the Flowers. They earned praise from outlets such as Paste Magazine, The Nashville Scene, Spill Magazine, and Americana UK while incessantly touring across America. Cutting their teeth on the road eventually paid off as Edens won runner-up at the esteemed Telluride Troubadour Songwriting competition in 2024. The veneer of a quiet songster singing breezy Nick Drake-esque melodies was quickly dashed after Edens lost their mother in late 2024 after a long journey with early-onset dementia. After releasing 2025’s lo-fi collection of voice memos it’s your birthday & you’re gorgeous with no fanfare or promotion, Edens disappeared from touring for the better part of a year. Some say Edens went out to New Mexico to find god. Others say Edens turned into a butterfly and floated south to greener pastures. Edens will say that they continued to find hope in writing songs.

Newly molded by the black hole of grief, the singer reemerges this fall with their first record in 4 years. Death Drive is the sound of someone finding themself while also losing control. Heavy and light, black and neon-tinged, the album is a masterful achievement of contemporary indie rock, poignantly moving through the landscape of grief while also foisting…

events.title: Joe Hunt Group
about: $15 admission / Start 8:30pm / Doors 8pm / Seated Show Modern jazz played by Boston's best jazz musicians.

Joe Hunt is a jazz drummer, educator, author, and historian. In the early 1960s, Joe Hunt performed and recorded alongside the late NEC Distinguished Artist-in-Residence Emeritus George Russell, with releases on Decca and Riverside. Hunt joined The Stan Getz Quartet in 1964, recording several releases on Verve, then was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1966-1967. The remainder of the 1960s found Hunt performing or recording with several other jazz luminaries including Chet Baker, Eric Dolphy, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Charles Mingus, Bob Brookmeyer, and the late Herb Pomeroy.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Hunt was a member of The National Jazz Ensemble, led jazz groups with John Scofield, Mike Stern, and Santi Debriano, and toured with quartets of Red Rodney and Hal McKusick. The 1990s, and beyond, have included membership in The Smithsonian Jazz Masters Orchestra, with former NEC president Gunther Schuller, performances with Kenny Burrell, Joe Lavano, Joanne Brackeen, and Tal Farlow, as well as recordings with the Bert Seager Quintet, and also, Trio. Hunt is the author of the 1994 book 52nd Street Beat, which is a historical look at jazz drummer greats from 1945 to 1965.

Mark Pinto - alto saxophone, formerly years with the Buddy Rich band John Lockwood – bass, formerly with Joe Henderson, Lee Konitz, current Fringe member Yuka Hamano Hunt – piano, voice, arranger Joe Hunt – drums, formerly with George Russell, Stan Getz, Jim Hall, Dexter Gordon, and Bill Evans We pay tribute to a special composer or performer at most performances. Recent shows have included: Burt Bacharach, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans, and Gigi Gryce. Future shows will include the music of Paul and Carla Bley, and arranger, Johnny Mandel.
Continuing of the 3rd Sunday of Every Month

events.title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi, Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray, Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest, Trumpet Double-click to edit...

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

events.title: The Fringe
about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone, bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood.
Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind.

Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow.
Continuing Every Monday at 10:30pm

about: Join Mic Drop for an open mic & karaoke of horror!

You can stay on theme with the horror or wander in whichever direction you choose, it is only a thought:) This is a space to perform, experiment, try something new, and find your people! Whether it be poetry, singing, playing an instrument, doing stand-up, dancing, improv-ing with nothing prepared, karaoking, or whatnot -- the stage is yours to make what you would like! Only one rule: have the funnest of funs. Come curious, come creative, and come cheer loud and proud!
6:15 Doors

6:15-6:45 Chill + Eat/Drink + Chat There is a cafe with plenty of great food and drink options to purchase, as well as time to meet new people and chill with your friends pre-show! There will also be a sign-up sheet upon entering for performers so you can list where in the set you would like to perform. Again, ANY act is welcome (singing, poetry, instrumentals, dancing, improv, stand up, doing a handstand, sea shantys, etc. etc. -- we encourage you to be as whimsy as you would like and to experiment and try something new if this is your first time!)

6:45-9:30 Open Mic, Hootenanny, & Karaoke We will kick off with our first performance at 7PM and each artist will have a max of 5 minutes of stage time to use as they wish (with the exception of setting the stage on fire or bringing a drumset). You do not have to use the full five minutes, but after the 5 minutes are over, we will [casually] nudge you off stage. This is to ensure that all individuals are given the opportunity to perform, no one gets too bored, and there is a variety of arts we all get to witness... You are also allowed to have a max of 3 people on the stage at once if you would like to perform something with your friends!

Things to Note: Please be mindful that there is no outside food or drinks welcome in the ROOTED Café. We also have to meet a minimum food/drink buy from the cafe so please take advantage of the incredible offerings 🍺🍸🍹🥂!!

events.title: The Bowery Presents Pokey LaFarge
about: Pokey LaFarge is coming to Arts at the Armory on November 10, 2026 to celebrate the release of his new album, 'Rent Money'. Grab your tickets now!

For two decades, Pokey LaFarge has walked his own effortlessly cool road as an exceptionally iconoclastic troubadour – forthright, genuine, and markedly keen to put it all out there. Rent Money now sees him pushing forward yet again in what can be safely declared his finest collection to date, both as an heartfelt expression of personal experience and as no-nonsense social commentary. With its twanging guitars, plucky rhythms, and undeniably captivating melodies, the album soars and swings, its joyous refrains belying the inescapable undercurrent of constant worry and angst that permeates these troubled times. As always, the Illinois native deftly traverses the genre boundaries, seamlessly integrating the myriad strains of 20th-century American music with a freewheeling command of earnest songcraft, inspired performance, and subversive creativity. Rent Money stands tall as an indisputable high-water mark for Pokey LaFarge – a defining collection from a one-of-a-kind artist of rare ingenuity and uncommon candor, now as ever, determinedly crafting a sure-footed brand of deeply human music all his own.

events.title: The Bowery Presents Liana Flores
about: Doors open at 7:00 PM · Show begins at 8:00 PM
“This record is the story of the country girl moving to the city,” Liana Flores says. “It’s bossa nova meets pop, inspired by the people, relationships and glamour of city life.”

Since the release of her acclaimed 2024 debut album Flower of the soul, British-Brazilian singer-songwriter Liana Flores has been at the forefront of a bossa nova revival. Drawing on the ‘60s sound of genre pioneers like Joao Gilberto alongside pop songwriting, Flores combines the dual aspects of her cultural heritage to create an emotive sound.

Following extensive tour dates across North America, Asia and Europe, Flores now returns with a new EP, And so it goes…, that expands her palette to encompass the playful and ebullient experiences of moving from her rural hometown in Norfolk to St. Andrews before coming to London. The result is a six track collection that shifts between finger-picked guitar and gossamer bossa vocals of “So it goes” to the upbeat funk inflections of the heavy-grooving love song “So mysterious”, the Carole King-influenced folk storytelling of “Here to stay,” and the sprightly, glittering pop melodies of “Silvershoes.”

“These songs were informed by my experiences living in the city and touring for the first time. I grew up and studied in small towns with nature in my surroundings, so that’s what came naturally in terms of lyrics. With So it goes, the lyrics are more centred on human connection, and I wanted to explore a part of my identity that’s more playful and matter-of-fact. I also wanted to challenge myself to write songs with strong melodies that would be fun to sing or to get ready to.”

Raised by an immigrant Brazilian mother and British father in East Anglia, Flores first began learning music while listening to ‘80s and ‘90s bossa nova artists like Bebel Gilberto and Leila Pinheiro alongside Top 40 pop radio. In her late teens, she picked up a guitar and started emulating finger-picked bossa nova guitar chords by ear, first covering Tom Jobim standards, then writing her own songs combining the bossa guitar style with her own introspective lyrics, expressing loneliness, self-doubt, and endurance.

events.title: Aga Khan Program Fall 2026 An Evening With Lecture Series: Anna Pronina: The “waqf question” in Soviet Turkestan and Architectural Restoration
about: Photo: Ernst Cohn-Wiener, Photo of the Madrasah-i Ulugh Beg in Samarkand, 1924-25 Source: The British museum In the early Soviet period, the preservation of Islamic architecture in Central Asia became entangled with a struggle over the property and revenues that had historically sustained it. This talk examines the relationship between Islamic charitable endowments and Soviet preservation agencies in Samarkand between 1922 and 1927, focusing on the activities of the Samarkand Commission for the Preservation and Restoration of Monuments and its parent institution, Turkomstaris. Facing chronic shortages of funding, Turkomstaris sought access to waqf revenues traditionally used to support mosques, madrasas, and shrines. Their claims brought them into conflict with the newly established Soviet waqf administration, as well as local Muslim communities and custodians of endowed property. These disputes raised fundamental questions about who controlled waqf resources, who had authority over Islamic buildings, and what constituted legitimate restoration. Drawing on archival records, administrative correspondence, and local press, the talk explores how preservationists, Soviet officials, and Muslim communities negotiated competing claims to waqf and architectural heritage and what argumentative strategies they used.

Anna is a cultural historian, curator, and researcher of the Soviet Union, specializing in Central Asia. She received her PhD in History from Central European University (Vienna). Her dissertation, Crafting Socialist Realism: Heritage, Materiality, and Expertise in Soviet Uzbekistan, 1930s–1950s, examines the production of architecture, opera, ballet, and visual arts in Soviet Uzbekistan, arguing that Socialist Realism emerged through negotiations among local experts, Soviet-trained professionals, and state institutions rather than through unilateral directives from Moscow. By foregrounding local knowledge and heritage, the study reconceptualizes Socialist Realism as a flexible and contested mode of cultural production. She co-curated the exhibition Split Together, Merged Apart (GES-2, Moscow, 2025), which examined Soviet archaeology and restoration practices in Central Asia, and served as an academic advisor to the first Bukhara Biennial of Contemporary Art. events.title: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch
about: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group Nikolaus Hirsch is co-founder and co-editor of e-flux Architecture, as well as the director of the museum Kanal Architecture (formerly CIVA) in Brussels. He was the Dean of Städelschule and Director of the Portikus in Frankfurt and taught at the Architectural Association in London. His architectural work includes the award-winning Dresden Synagogue, Hinzert Document Center, Bockenheimer Depot Theater (with William Forsythe), Cybermohalla Hub in New-Delhi, “Do We Dream Under The Same Sky“(with Rirkrit Tiravanija at Art Basel / LUMA Arles) and “Becoming Monument” in Fukushima. Hirsch has curated numerous exhibitions such “Wohnungsfrage / Housing Question” at the HKW in Berlin and the German Pavilion at the Architecture Biennale in Venice (“2038”). He is the editor of the Critical Spatial Practice series at Sternberg Press.

Nick Axel is an architect, editor, educator, and curator. As Deputy Editor of e-flux Architecture, he has led the development of the platform since its founding in 2016 and undertaken more than 60 editorial projects and publications in collaboration with biennials, museums, universities, and other cultural and research institutions around the world. Nick is also Head of the Architectural Design department at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam, a three-year educational program at the intersection of architecture, research, theory, and art. He was recently Editor of the 19th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, curated by Carlo Ratti, and from 2020–2022, was Curator of Architecture and Chair of the Architectural Advisory Board at the Babyn Yar Holocaust Memorial Center, Kyiv. He has edited numerous books, including most recently: Sick Architecture (MIT Press, 2025), with Beatriz Colomina, Guillermo S. Arsuaga, and e-flux Architecture; Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. (La Biennale di Venezia, 2025); Chronograms of Architecture (Spector Books, 2025), with Silvia Franceschini, Lily Jencks, Nikolaus Hirsch, and Eszter Steierhoffer; and Concéntrico: Urban Innovation Laboratory (Park Books, 2025), with Javier Peña Ibáñez.

events.title: The Need for Roots in a Digital Society | Catherine D’Ignazio
about: On November 6, Boston University’s Center for Media Innovation & Social Impact hosts its second Annual Summit. The day-long event will feature speakers, workshops, and panel discussions across disciplines and between city, university, and community members to investigate the pressing issues related to attention, ecology, community, and trust.

AI systems increasingly guide decisions that play out in local contexts: who gets flagged as a risk, whose neighborhood gets patrolled or invested in, whose voice counts in a dispute. The criminal justice system is one prominent example, but the pattern recurs across many domains where data built and trained far from a community ends up shaping outcomes within it. This panel explores what it means to build systems that are answerable to the communities most affected by them.

Panelists will consider what normative questions about fairness and accountability get decided, often invisibly, in technical design choices; and how local, community rooted approaches to justice can push back against technologies built at scale and at a distance. Ultimately, the question is: in the formal and informal spaces of public life, whose knowledge counts, and who gets to decide?

events.title: MIT Henge 2026
about: Observe the sun as it aligns with the Infinite Corridor!

Tuesday, November 10, at approximately 4:19:23 pm Light refreshments to follow in Lobby 13 Watch Professor Post-Tenure Richard Binzel explain this unique piece of MIT's lore in this video short about MIT Henge!

Warning: The fact that the sun is at the horizon does not mean that it is safe to look at for more than a moment. Do not injure your eyes by staring at the sun. Use appropriate filters or glance only for a moment as you would at the sun up in the sky.
View from the Building 8 end. Don’t go up to the Building 7/Mass. Ave. end of the corridor. You won’t see anything special there, and you will prevent others from seeing.

Arrive early and don’t block the corridor. Especially given the apparent systematic tendency for predictions to be 5-8 minutes late, it’s best to arrive 15 minutes early. This helps make sure you’re not trying to scramble for a spot and blocking somebody else’s view. Above all, do not walk in the corridor in front of all the people trying to catch a glimpse of the sun.

Don’t leave until the very end. People who take a picture in the middle and then leave block the corridor for those still observing. Some people observe for the entire span in which the sun is even barely visible; leaving early blocks their view.

Use the third floor. The 3rd floor has the best view because it has an uninterrupted sweep of corridor, and because it is the highest usable floor. You can’t see anything from the fourth floor because it doesn’t go through.
Let others see. Not very many people can get a good view of this phenomenon at once. Once you have seen, get out of the way and let others look.

Stand in the stairwell. The place that has the largest unobstructed angle of view of the sky is the stairwell just below the third floor. Get your eye right by the edge of corridor floor. Great view? Now give someone else a chance.
Don’t hurt your eyes. See the warning above.
Read more info on Infinite Corridor astronomy!

events.title: History of Now Lectures Series - A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948
about: History at MIT invites you to join us on Thursday, November 19th at 5 pm in E51-095 for the final lecture in the History of Now series, featuring Orit Bashkin, the Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History and Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields at the University of Chicago. Her talk is titled "A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948."
Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields University of Chicago Thursday, November 19, 2026
5-6:30 pm · MIT Building E51, Room 095

Orit Bashkin is a historian who works on the intellectual, social, and cultural history of the modern Middle East. She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. Since her graduation, she has been working as a professor of modern Middle Eastern history in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago. Her publications deal with Iraqi history, the history of Iraqi Jews, the Arab cultural revival movement (the nahda) in the late 19th century, and the connections between modern Arab history and Arabic literature. Her current research project explores the lives of Iraqi Jews in Israel.
All of these lectures are free and open to the public. More information on the lecture series is available here.

about: Colectivo C733—Gabriella Carrillo and Carlos Facio (in collaboration with the Norman B. Leventhal Center for Advanced Urbanism)

events.title: MIT Music Tech Speaker Series Presents: Mark Ethier
about: Tools for Musicians in the Age of AI: From iZotope to Berklee Music and technology have always co-evolved. Long before the synthesizer, innovations ranging from new tuning systems to the piano's sustain pedal haven’t just made music easier to produce — they’ve fundamentally changed what kind of music is possible to make. How will AI as an underlying technology fit into this history?

Since I was an undergraduate at MIT, I’ve spent my career building tools for musicians and watching this interplay firsthand. Sometimes, new technology inspires the music itself, like how rhythmic delay helped inspire U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name.” Other times, musicians drive the technology. At iZotope, our collaboration with BT on Stutter Edit took intricate audio effects that could require hours of studio editing and made them playable in real time onstage.

I’ve also witnessed the impact of the democratization of music making. We helped build a path for musicians to launch careers from their bedrooms, but we also watched large-format studios close their doors. It’s too early to fully grasp how generative AI will impact creative possibilities and livelihoods, but I'll share some early signals from recent market research, including Berklee’s June 2026 report, In Sync: Music and Video 2026.

Now, we’re entering a new phase: the democratization of tool building. With a quiet revolution of musicians vibe-coding their own tools, this story is far from over. In these moments of change, it’s often clear what is being lost. But we also have to wonder what new artistic expression becomes possible, and with the evolution of generative AI, question who gets to shape that change and benefit from it.

Mark Ethier is an entrepreneur and innovator dedicated to empowering creativity. In 2001, after graduating from MIT with degrees in music and computer science, he cofounded iZotope. Today, he is the Founding Executive Director of Berklee's Emerging Artistic Technology Lab (BEATL) helping musicians navigate technology.

Under Mark’s leadership as CEO, iZotope’s tools helped musicians, engineers, and producers realize their creative vision and earned numerous honors, including multiple NAMM TEC Awards (Technical Excellence & Creativity), two Primetime Engineering Emmy Awards for Outstanding Achievement in Engineering Development, and an Academy Award for Scientific and Engineering Achievement.…

events.title: Author Talk: A Pox on Fools
about: Join us for an engaging evening with author Thomas Levenson as he discusses his new book, "A Pox on Fools: The True Believers, Grifters, and Cynics Who Convinced Us to Reject Vaccines," in conversation with MIT Museum Director Michael John Gorman.

Since the advent of smallpox inoculation in the eighteenth century, the idea that a disease introduced to the body in some lesser, weakened form might prevent full-blown infection has been one of the greatest public health insights of the modern era, inspiring the invention of numerous vaccines and saving countless human lives. But, just as humanity acquired the superhuman ability to stop infectious disease in its tracks, some feared we had gone too far, leading to skepticism that has hijacked public health discourse today.

In three sweeping essays written for our current moment of scientific mistrust, Thomas Levenson searches for the origins of the most common arguments against vaccines: that they are unnatural; that they are more dangerous than the illnesses they claim to prevent; and that they are an affront to freedom. Each arose from the earliest development of particular vaccines and the campaigns to distribute them. Even as the pattern repeats, Levenson reveals how innocent that skepticism initially was and, in each case, how very human fears and questions ultimately turned into something darker, where no truth would be enough to overcome the doubt.

events.title: Co-Adaptive—Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston
about: Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group As our planet gets hotter, and more extreme weather events become the norm, CO Adaptive is positioning themselves as an unbuild, design and build practice: a new model that reunites designers and builders through collaboration in order to re-think our joint role in shaping the built environment; contending with architecture at the intersection of saving embodied carbon and reducing operational energy. As stewards of the existing material repository contained in our cities, CO Adaptive aims to increase the resilience and reusability of all that already surrounds us.

Their talk will engage the breadth of the practice’s work—from adaptive reuse projects and high-efficiency retrofits to material salvage operations, remanufacturing, and design for disassembly. These projects yield a critical perspective on how buildings and materials re-engage in their next iteration of use, working towards a reality in which extractive and depleting habits are replaced by a circular library of abundance.

CO Adaptive is an unbuild-design-build practice founded by Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston in 2011. Initially it was started as an architecture practice, focused on retrofitting existing building stock to create energy efficient, climate resilient and spatially beautiful environments.

To have a greater impact on the process of taking old buildings apart—emphasizing deconstruction, and shaping attitudes about “waste”—CO Adaptive Building was established in 2021 and CO Adaptive Disassembly in 2026. The attention of all three intertwined practices is on converting existing buildings from a linear economy to a circular one.

CO Adaptive’s work has received numerous awards and recognition, including winning the Architectural League’s Emerging Voices 2026, A|N’s 2025 Best of Practice Award, and the 2025 Trust for Governors Island Climate Solutions Challenge. Their adaptive reuse project for The Mercury Store was featured in MoMA’s Inaugural New York New Publics exhibition and won the MASterworks Design Award for Adaptive Reuse in 2023. Ruth and Bobby are frequent lecturers on circular design, have taught a graduate design studio at Columbia GSAPP, and are excited to be teaching a studio at MIT this fall.

events.title: Author Talk: Linford D. Fisher — Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in U.S. History
about: Join author Linford Fisher in a discussion of his book, Stealing America, where he shows that although the first enslaved Africans arrived in Jamestown in 1619, European slavery in America began more than a century before.

The enslavement of Indigenous people began in the years just after 1492, ensnaring an estimated three to six million Natives throughout the Americas. Although largely erased from the public consciousness, Native enslavement continued for centuries to become a colossal phenomenon that affected nearly 600,000 Native Americans in North America alone, revealing the shocking truth that American colonizers enslaved Natives in roughly the same numbers as they imported enslaved Africans.

From Virginia to California, from New England to Barbados, Stealing America traces the history of Indigenous enslavement and land dispossession, detailing how colonizers captured Natives and often deliberately mislabeled them as Black slaves to avoid detection. While the American Revolution pealed the bells of freedom for colonists, it paved a larcenous trail of westward expansion that subsequently plundered Indigenous land and stole the labor of Natives from nations like the Cherokee, Navajo, Nisean, and many others. “This double theft,” Fisher writes, “was central to the origins, growth, and eventual success of the English colonies and the United States—not just initially but throughout all of American history.”

Fisher will weave together accounts of major episodes in American history including early colonization, the American Revolution, and the Civil War with lesser-known stories of Native enslavement and land loss. Fisher upends conventional histories about the nature of American slavery, revealing enslaved Natives in places we have overlooked, including southern antebellum plantations and the nineteenth-century American West. After Congress outlawed Native slavery in 1867, Americans forced Indigenous children into boarding schools and white homes, where they labored under forced assimilation. This practice was not reformed until the latter twentieth century, when Native nations finally secured increasing rights and self-determination.

Linford D. Fisher is an associate professor of history at Brown University. The author of The Indian Great Awakening and principal investigator of the Stolen Relations project, he lives in Providence, Rhode Island.

events.title: Author Talk: Laura Zigman — The Author Weekend
about: The Fall 2026 Author Talk Series, presented by the Friends of the South End Library, will continue with Laura Zigman sharing about her latest novel, The Author Weekend. Please join us on Wednesday, November 11 starting at 6:30 pm at Union Church (Connection Room, 485 Columbus Ave.) for a fun and lively conversation in this author talk series!

Everything needs to be just right for bestselling mystery writer Faye Wader's first ever fan weekend. Her sales might be slipping––only a little!––but her readers still love her enough to pony up for three days and two nights on Great Misery Island. The retreat is precisely planned, from the small batch artisanal donuts to the perimenopausal Mermaid Meditation, by Faye and her beleaguered assistant Jade––an aspiring author who can't seem to finish her own novel. Faye's long-time agent and editor will be there, as well as Faye's number one fan, Peggy Mercer, who has been first in line at every one of Faye's events. When news comes that the weekend will be crashed by glamorous, charismatic, rival novelist Abby Schuss, Faye thinks things can't get worse... until one of the attendees is found dead in her room, setting off an unexpectedly murderous chain of events that make pre-pub anxiety seem like a day at the beach. How far is Faye willing to go to get exactly what she wants from her author weekend? The Author Weekend is a thrilling and hilarious dive into the dark heart of envy, and a glorious exploration of a woman of a certain age desperate to survive the dog-eat-dog world of publishing and control her own narrative.

Laura Zigman is the author of Small World, Separation Anxiety, Animal Husbandry, Dating Big Bird, Her, and Piece of Work. She has collaborated on several works of nonfiction—including Eddie Izzard’s New York Times bestseller, Believe Me—and has been a contributor to The New York Times and other publications.

events.title: Art Exhibition — Rachel King: At the Water's Edge
about: The Jamaica Plain Branch Library, in partnership with the Friends of the Jamaica Plain Branch of the Boston Public Library, is pleased to present At the Water’s Edge, the next exhibition of its 2026 rotating art series, featuring photography by Jamaica Plain artist Rachel King.

At the Water’s Edge traces the seasonal shifts along the shore of Jamaica Pond. Working in the field of addiction and recovery, King began turning to photography in the wake of the overdose epidemic, intensified by COVID-19, as a way to connect more deeply with her local landscape and community. What began as documenting the familiar evolved into a daily photographic journal, an exercise in slowing down and paying attention to small changes that can easily go unnoticed.

King was drawn to the water’s edge, where waves, melting ice, changing light, and reflections continually alter the landscape, transforming recognizable forms into unexpected patterns and abstract shapes.The daily practice also became a way of marking time. Each image captures conditions that may never recur in quite the same way; together, they form a record not only of a changing landscape, but of the act of looking itself.

Through At the Water’s Edge, King invites viewers to look closely at a place that may already feel familiar, and to consider how sustained attention can reveal new ways of seeing even a landscape we know well.

At the Water’s Edge is on view from November 12, 2026–January 6, 2027, with a public reception to be held on Thursday, November 12, 2026, 5:30-7:30 PM. The library is open Monday-Wednesday 10-6, Thursday 12-8, and Friday and Saturday 9-5 (closed Sundays). The exhibition space is located on the lower level.

This exhibition is made possible through the generous support of The Friends of the Jamaica Plain Branch Library, a volunteer, community-based organization that seeks to enhance public awareness, recognition, status and financial support of the library system through advocacy and education.

events.title: Author Talk: Lauren Klein and Tanvi Sharma on "Data by Design"
about: Join visualization historian Lauren Klein and designer Tanvi Sharma for a conversation about their new book Data by Design: Visualization and Power from Abolition to the Dawn of Data Science. The book returns to the history of data visualization to expose the power of charts and maps—and to show how they can be used for social change. Lauren and Tanvi will be in conversation with Arvind Satyanarayan, a professor of data visualization at MIT.

​Lauren Klein is Professor of Data & Decision Sciences and English at Emory University, where she also directs the Digital Humanities Lab and the Atlanta Interdisciplinary AI Network. Her research brings together computational and critical methods to explore questions of gender, race, and justice, both in early America and today. Klein is the author (with Catherine D’Ignazio) of the award-winning Data Feminism (MIT Press, 2020), and the editor (with Matthew K. Gold) of Debates in the Digital Humanities (Univ. of Minnesota Press), among other publications.

​Tanvi Sharma is a design technologist working at the intersection of data, aesthetics, and the humanities. She is currently an Art Director at Apple and co-author of Data by Design (MIT Press, 2026). She has previously worked at Pentagram, Public Policy Lab, and Spotify. She lives in Harlem, NY, with her two cats, Yuchi and Bubbles. More at tanvi.network.

​Arvind Satyanarayan is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at MIT EECS, and leads the Visualization Group at the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). His research uses visualization as a petri dish to study intelligence augmentation (IA), or how computation can amplify our cognition and creativity, while respecting our agency. Open-source visualization systems developed by Arvind and his collaborators are widely used by researchers, companies, and journalists. Arvind’s research has been recognized with several awards including, most recently, an Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship.

events.title: Before Salem: Witchcraft in Boston’s North End, 1688: Cotton Mather, Martha Goodwin, and the Making of a Witchcraft Panic
about: Join the Friends of the North End Branch Library in welcoming James Pasto for Before Salem: Witchcraft in Boston’s North End, 1688: Cotton Mather, Martha Goodwin, and the Making of a Witchcraft Panic.

In 1688, Boston’s North End was the scene of one of New England’s most famous witchcraft cases. Four children of the Goodwin family were believed to have been bewitched, and Cotton Mather, one of Boston’s leading Puritan ministers, became closely involved in the case. This talk examines the Goodwin case within the broader history of Puritan Boston and the beliefs, fears, and social tensions that shaped accusations of witchcraft. Drawing on insights from cultural anthropology, it explores how witchcraft beliefs function in different societies, why accusations arise, and how the events in Boston helped set the stage for the Salem witchcraft trials of 1692.
Presented by James S. Pasto, Ph.D.

events.title: Author Talk: Maria Termini — Available Details
about: Join local Author Maria Termini as she reads from her new book Available Details: Wonder, Adventure and More!

Available Details: Adventure, Wonder and More (Memoir) contains thirty-one stories from my rich life of many varied experiences. I have imagined myself to be reporting live and with all the abundant details at the scene of certain events and times in my life. From an early age, I was gifted with curiosity, imagination and this has led me to many diverse travels and pursuits. Collecting postage stamps and devouring the colorful pages of National Geographic magazines inspired me with a lifelong desire for adventure that would not be dimmed by my lack of money or the demands of single motherhood. I discovered gold at age nine, volunteered to be Lady Godiva at twenty, learned figure skating at fifty, found enchantment in the Boston Public Schools, traveled to Morocco and Sicily with my twin sons, lived in the White Mountain National Forest, did carpentry work in Hawaii, joined the Peace Corps, hiked on the Appalachian Trail and so many other things. In the patchwork quilt of my life the random pieces work harmoniously together in the unfinished art work that is my life and always with wonder, adventure and joy. Tune into this book and be inspired to follow your own dreams.

events.title: Author Talk — Alex Krieger: Greenhorn
about: Join local author Alex Krieger as he reads from and discusses his new memoir Greenhorn: Episodes in an Immigrant's Life. It explores a life shaped by motion, memory, cultures and careers, which unfolds in the art of making a home in the unfamiliar. At the age of nine, Alex Krieger arrived in America with his three parents—survivors of the Holocaust. In Chicago, he finds his fourth first-grade classroom to learn a fourth language in four years. From displaced childhood, the journeying continues as teacher, architect, planner of cities. With a poet's sensitivity and a craftsman's precision, Krieger reflects on that greenhorn's instinct to embrace the values of an adopted nation while remaining eyewitness to paradoxes.

Alex Krieger is Professor Emeritus at the Harvard Graduate School of Design where he taught since 1977. An architect, planner and author, he has directed design and planning projects in American and international cities, including the reconstruction of the Bund in Shanghai. Former chair of the Department of Urban Planning and Design, he remains an advisor to public and educational institutions, including two terms on the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. He is a founding board member of the Leventhal Map & Education Center and the co-author of Mapping Boston.

events.title: The Artist’s Voice: Leilah Babirye with Ruth Erickson
about: “Reusing materials is important to me, as a person who comes from a background where the LGBTQ community is looked at as trash still today. As an artist, I find beauty in using found materials to showcase and reclaim my community.” -Leilah Babirye Bicycle chains, gears, and tire tubes are some of the unexpected elements in Leilah Babirye’s latest sculptures at the ICA. Her art, celebrating a one-of-a-kind queer wedding, depicts attendees of this special life event through ceramic and carved wood sculptures. Join Babirye and ICA’s Barbara Lee Chief Curator Ruth Erickson as they reflect on the artist’s unique practice that proudly reclaims space, identity, and community through art. This program explores Babirye’s many creative influences from African sculpture to found object art and addresses cultural and political systems of oppression embedded in Uganda, including the Anti-Homosexuality Act (2014/2023) that endangers and criminalizes many lives.

Make the most of your ICA visit! Explore Leilah Babirye’s ICA exhibition and stop by Art-Making After Dark for a hands-on activity designed by the artist and enjoy a drink and light bite in the waterfront Wine + Coffee Bar after the talk.
Free

events.title: Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company: Collage Revisited and Story/
about: The Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company return to the ICA with a program reflecting on history, legacy, and continued experimentation.

In Collage Revisited, the full company revisits The History of Collage, the last collaboration between Bill T. Jones and Arnie Zane before Arnie’s death. Originally created in 1988, the remounting is part of a legacy project for the company — looking back to look forward. The piece recalls the excitement the two artists shared as they set out to reconsider dance spectacle during the 1980s art scene. Collage Revisited blends dance, music, and spoken word, exploring themes of identity.
$45 ICA members / $50 students / $60 nonmembers

events.title: Gallery Talk: Max Gruber on 90 YEARS
about: Founded in 1936, the ICA is one of the oldest museums dedicated to contemporary art in the United States. On this special anniversary, 90 YEARS revisits nine exhibitions and initiatives from the ICA’s history, tracing the museum’s evolution alongside the ever-changing landscape of contemporary art. Join Curatorial Assistant Max Gruber for a conversation about pivotal moments in the ICA’s history with a focus on the landmark 1941 exhibition Modern Mexican Painters.

Max Gruber is Curatorial Assistant at the Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston. He has contributed to several ICA exhibitions, including Tau Lewis: Spirit Level, The Gun Violence Memorial Project, Charles Atlas: About Time, and An Indigenous Present. Before joining the ICA, Gruber contributed to the exhibition and accompanying publication for Humane Ecology: Eight Positions at the Clark Art Institute. He holds an M.A. in the History of Art from Williams College.
Free with museum admission <div

events.title: Peter Pan Syndrome
about: Inspired by the tales of J.M. Barrie, Dmitry Krymov's "Peter Pan. Syndrome" is about art and the artist – the creator who, even when trapped in a dead end, when despair tightens around the throat and the urge to abandon everything feels unbearable, still returns to creation. Overcoming pain, he, like Peter Pan, cannot grow up from his passion for art; he continues to make miracles because he knows no other way to live. You want to let him go, to say, "Rest!" – but he is so radiant, his miracles so beautiful, and his heart so full of love that the audience, weeping, cannot bring themselves to release him.

Presented in Latvian w/ Russian subtitles Running time: 1 hour 45 minutes Directed by Dmitry Krymov Set Design by Dmitry Krymov, Uģis Bērziņš Video artist: Toms Zeļģis Lighting Design by Oskars Pauliņš ABOUT THE DIRECTOR DMITRY KRYMOV Known for his innovative, design-centric style, Dmitry Krymov is one of the most original directorial voices of his generation. He has been hailed as “one of the world’s finest theatermakers” (New York Times), and has won several awards for his work, both in Russia and internationally. In early 2022, Krymov was in Philadelphia, preparing his production of The Cherry Orchard, which was scheduled to premiere at the Wilma Theatre in February. After Russia invaded Ukraine, he condemned the invasion and refused to return to his homeland. In October 2022, Krymov announced the opening of his new studio in New York City – Krymov Lab NYC.

events.title: Behind the Screen: La Bola Negra
about: LA BOLA NEGRA, the bold new film from Spanish writer-directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, won the Best Director award at Cannes and the People's Choice award at the Toronto International Film Festival. Inspired by the surviving pages of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca and by Alberto Conejero's award-winning play La piedra oscura, the film tells the interconnected stories of three gay men in Spain in 1932, 1937, and 2017. Moving from the years before the Spanish Civil War, through the war itself, to the present day, LA BOLA NEGRA is a sweeping, passionate triptych about desire, repression, historical memory, and what one generation carries forward to the next.
Our panel will explore the film's roots in Lorca's work, its portrayal of the Spanish Civil War and the Franco era, and how it brings queer history and historical memory to the screen.

Margaret E. Deffenbaugh and LeRoy T. Carlson Professor in Comparative Literary Studies and Professor of Spanish, Wellesley College Carlos Ramos's teaching and research focus on the literature and cultural history of contemporary Spain. His published work includes Construyendo la modernidad: Escritura y arquitectura en el Madrid moderno (1918-1937) and Poesía insomne.

Associate Professor of Hispanic Studies, Boston College Wan Sonya Tang teaches courses on Spanish literature and culture from the nineteenth century onward. She is the author of Specters, Monsters, and the Damned: Fantastic Threats to the Social Order in 19th-Century Spain and co-editor of Televising Restoration Spain, which examines how heritage film and television explore Spain's relationship to modernity in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
Professor of Hispanic Studies and Comparative Literature, Brandeis University Fernando Rosenberg is the author of After Human Rights: Literature, Visual Arts, and Film in Latin America, 1990-2010.
Directed by Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo · 2h 35m

events.title: Behind the Screen: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
about: ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM captures an extraordinary evening in 1972, when pioneering documentarian William Greaves gathered surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance at Duke Ellington's Harlem townhouse. Over four hours, artists, writers, and intellectuals, many of whom had not seen one another in fifty years, reminisced, argued, laughed, and debated their place in a rapidly changing cultural landscape. Greaves considered it the most important event he ever filmed. Decades later, his son David Greaves, one of the original camera operators, restored the 16mm footage and completed the film, creating both a vivid time capsule and a searching inquiry into one of the most creative periods in American history.

Our panelists will discuss the Harlem Renaissance and its legacy, the remarkable figures gathered in Greaves's footage, and the story of how this film was made and, fifty years later, finally completed.

Kendra Taira Field is the Gerald R. Gill Associate Professor of History and Director of the Center for Public History at Tufts University; and a 2025-26 Hutchins Fellow at Harvard University. A citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, Field is the author of Growing Up with the Country (Yale, 2018), which traced her own ancestors’ post emancipation lives in Indian Territory and Oklahoma. Field’s American Historical Review article, "The Privilege of Family History" explores the history of African American engagement with family history and genealogy in slavery and freedom. Field abridged David Levering Lewis' W.E.B. Du Bois: A Biography (Henry Holt, 2009) and co-founded the Du Bois Forum, a retreat for writers, scholars, and artists. Field serves as Chief Historian for the 10 Million Names Project and has appeared in numerous historical documentaries and television programs, including Henry Louis Gates, Jr.'s "The African Americans: Many Rivers to Cross" (2013) and HBO Max’s, Breaking New Ground

Professor of the Practice, Theatre, Dance, and Performance Studies, Tufts University Khary Jones is Professor of the Practice, Theatre, Dance, and Performance Studies at Tufts University. As a writer-director, his work includes the award-winning documentary Night Fight and the short films Hug, Three and a Half Thoughts, and Chrysalis. He has also served on the editorial teams behind the documentary features Where the Pavement Ends; Black Memorabilia; Lorraine…
Directed by William Greaves, David Greaves · 1h 40m
